rv.q: This enjoyable and unsettling show, directed with panache by Blanche McIntyre, is a must-see – above all, for Denis O'Hare's Tartuffe, who is comic and dangerous – an unforgettable mix.
“I want things to be how they were when I was young,” the character explains, outlining the appeal of Tartuffe’s kindness. That definitely ties in with Brexit but its relevance is wider.
There is plenty to like, and laugh at, here. O'Hare, in particular, is brilliant as the bendy faux yogi Tartuffe.
Blanche McIntyre's lavish production takes a while to exert its grip.
But this is a sustained comic turn by O'Hare.
McIntyre, making her National Theatre debut, draws strong performances from her cast, but the satire feels muddy and the final swerve in tone is too abrupt.
Ferocious is probably the right description with its caustic modernist cultural references and pointed jabs at self-made men who create feckless off-spring then chastise them for being useless.

Here's a recipe for a successful National Theatre production: take a well-loved classical comedy, employ an outstanding young director and a talented writer (so much the better if they have a proven track record together) and cast gold-standard actors, including, if possible, someone with a screen presence.
